title: My Weirdly Good Pear Tallow Balm Routine (It’s Not What You Think)
body:
Okay so I’m just sitting here, it’s like 9 PM maybe, and I just put this stuff on my face. My phone’s at 12% and I’m half-watching some cooking show rerun. The stuff is this whipped tallow balm. Pear scent. Sounds insane, right? Beef fat for your face. I thought it was a joke. My friend sent me a link to this Etsy shop last month when I was complaining about my skin feeling like sandpaper. It was spring but my face didn’t get the memo. Still tight, still flaky. I ordered it because I was desperate and honestly, a little curious. The whole beef tallow skincare thing kept popping up. So I got the jar. It showed up in this little box, no fancy packaging. I opened it and just stared. This is what I paid for.

Anyway. Here’s what I actually do with it.

## How This Tallow Balm Fits in My Messy Evenings

My routine is not a routine. It’s a series of events that sometimes happen. But this balm has become a thing. A regular thing. After I wash my face—which I do with this cheap drugstore cleanser, the blue one—I pat it dry. Not all the way. A little damp. Then I scoop out a bit of this tallow balm. The amount is like… half a pea? Maybe a small pea. You don’t need much. It’s this whipped beef tallow balm, made from grass-fed suet apparently, whipped up in France. Feels fancy saying that. I rub it between my fingers to warm it up. It doesn’t melt like butter, more like it softens. Becomes this silky… I don’t know. Oil? Balm. Then I just press it into my skin. Mostly my cheeks and forehead. My nose gets a little. I avoid my eyes because, obviously.

The smell is subtle. Not like a candy pear. Not like a candle. It’s just this light, fresh, kinda fruity thing. It’s there for a second and then it’s gone. It’s nice. Sophisticated, I guess? My bathroom smelled like it for a minute. Then my cat walked in and started meowing at the sink, so that was the end of that thought.

Sometimes I use it in the morning if I’m not going anywhere. A tiny bit. It sinks in after like, ten minutes. Doesn’t leave me shiny. Just… hydrated. That’s the word. My skin drinks it. I read somewhere that beef tallow mimics human sebum so it absorbs deep. Makes sense. My skin knows what to do with it. Unlike that $80 cream I bought once that just sat on top feeling gross.

## Why I Even Gave Beef Tallow a Shot

Look, I was skeptical. Putting rendered beef fat on my face sounded like a prank. Or something my great-grandmother might have done. But winter wrecked my hands. Like, cracks near the knuckles, rough patches. I tried everything. Lotions, ointments, gloves overnight. Temporary fix. I saw this jar and figured, it’s for rough hands too. So one night, after doing the dishes, I globbed some on my hands. Like, a lot. Put on some old cotton socks as makeshift gloves and went to bed. Felt ridiculous.

Woke up. Washed my hands. And they were… different. Softer. The cracks were less angry. Not healed, but calmer. I did it again the next night. And again. After a week, my hands weren’t a disaster zone. That’s when I thought, okay, maybe the face thing isn’t so crazy.

So I started using the tallow balm on my face too. Just at night. I’d watch TV with it on. My skin felt… protected. Not greasy. Weird. Good weird. I started looking forward to it. The little ritual. Scoop, warm, press. It became the last thing I did before my brain shut off. A signal that the day was done. My skin felt plump in the morning. Not puffy, just… happy. The fine lines around my eyes, the ones I get when I’m dehydrated, looked less like canyons. More like faint pencil marks.

I got sidetracked looking at my hands just now. They’re okay. Not perfect. But okay. The balm lives on my nightstand now. Next to a water glass and a hair tie. It’s part of the landscape.

## What Actually Changed After a Few Weeks

I’m not gonna say it’s magic. It’s not. But my skin is just more resilient now. The spring wind used to make it sting. Now it doesn’t. I wore less makeup last week because I didn’t feel like I needed to cover up dry patches. That’s a win. The pear tallow balm is just this quiet background player. It doesn’t scream results. It just… works. It’s become my daily skincare with tallow, I guess. I don’t have a ten-step routine. I have this and a cleanser. And sunscreen. Always sunscreen.

My mom visited and asked what I was using. I showed her the jar. She made a face. “Beef fat?” I told her to just try it on her elbows. She did. Texted me two days later asking for the Etsy link. So I sent it to her. The shop is just this small operation. Nothing corporate. I like that.

Would I buy it again? I already did. I’m on my second jar. The first one lasted over two months, using it almost every night. That’s pretty good. It’s not cheap, but it’s not crazy expensive either. And it works better than things that cost three times as much. For me, that’s the whole point. Finding something simple that actually does the thing it says it will.

## Quick Questions I Get Asked

**Is beef tallow good for your face?**
Yeah, I think so. For me it is. From what I understand, it’s similar to the oils our skin makes naturally. So it gets absorbed instead of sitting on top. It feels like it’s helping my skin barrier, not just masking the problem.

**Does tallow balm clog pores?**
Hasn’t clogged mine. And my skin can get congested. It absorbs pretty well. I use a small amount. If you slather on a ton of anything, you might have issues. But a pea-sized bit for the whole face? Sinks right in.

**What does the pear tallow balm smell like?**
It’s light. A fresh, clean pear scent. Not sugary or artificial. It’s there when you open the jar and fades fast once it’s on your skin. It’s nice. Uncomplicated.

Anyway. That’s my tallow balm routine. No grand philosophy. Just a thing I do now that makes my skin feel less like it’s fighting me. If your skin’s being difficult, maybe give it a look. I got mine from a little Etsy shop. It’s just a simple jar of stuff that works. And sometimes, that’s enough.
